stages.name: Observe
stages.instruction: Move the $R$ and $C$ sliders. Watch the Bode magnitude curve rise from left to right. The purple marker sits on the cutoff frequency $f_c$ (where $|H| = -3\,\text{dB}$). Above $f_c$ the filter passes; below, it attenuates at $+20\,\text{dB/décade}$. Advance after visiting at least $3$ different $f_c$ decades.
stages.concept: A first-order CR high-pass has transfer function $|H(f)| = (f/f_c)/\sqrt{1 + (f/f_c)^2}$, with cutoff $f_c = 1/(2\pi\,R\,C)$. In decibels: $|H|_{\text{dB}} = 10\,\log_{10}\!\bigl((f/f_c)^2/(1 + (f/f_c)^2)\bigr)$. The gain rises at $+20\,\text{dB/décade}$ far below $f_c$, is $-3\,\text{dB}$ at $f_c$, then flattens to $\approx 0\,\text{dB}$ above.

stages.name: Experiment
stages.instruction: A microphone signal is contaminated by $50\,\text{Hz}$ mains hum. Adjust $R$ and $C$ to place the cutoff at the target frequency shown by the dashed orange line ($f_c = 200\,\text{Hz}$) so the hum is attenuated while the voice band passes. Many $(R, C)$ pairs work — you need $R\,C = 1/(2\pi\,f_c)$.
stages.concept: Design formula: $f_c = 1/(2\pi\,R\,C)$, so $R\,C = 1/(2\pi\,f_c)$. For $f_c = 200\,\text{Hz}$ you need $R\,C \approx 7.96\times10^{-4}\,\text{s}$ ($796\,\mu\text{s}$). Example combinations: $R = 8\,\text{k}\Omega$ with $C = 100\,\text{nF}$, or $R = 800\,\Omega$ with $C = 1\,\mu\text{F}$. What matters is the product, not the individual values. A common use: $C$ blocks DC and low-frequency hum, $R$ sets the corner.

stages.name: Evaluate
stages.instruction: Component values are hidden. Read $f_c$ directly from the Bode magnitude curve — it is where $|H|$ crosses $-3\,\text{dB}$, or equivalently the corner where the $+20\,\text{dB/décade}$ rising slope meets the flat region. Answer all questions correctly in one pass.
stages.concept: Reading $f_c$ off a Bode plot: find where the curve is $3\,\text{dB}$ below the pass-band gain (the $-3\,\text{dB}$ horizontal line is drawn). Alternatively, the intersection of the two asymptotes (rising side-line and flat top-line) is exactly $f_c$. Both methods give the same answer.

labels.question: question
labels.evaluate_prompt: Component values are hidden. Read f_c from the Bode plot alone.
labels.tip1: R↑ or C↑ → f_c shifts left ; f_c = 1/(2π·R·C)
labels.tip2: adjust R·C until the purple marker sits on the orange line
labels.tip3: read f_c off the plot where |H| = −3 dB — all must pass
labels.peek_tip_1: At f = f_c the gain drops to 1/√2 (−3 dB). Find the knee and read the x-axis.
labels.peek_tip_2: The −3 dB reference line is drawn. Follow the curve to where it crosses.
labels.peek_tip_3: The asymptote intersection is exactly f_c — trace the rising and flat lines to their meeting point.

1.1: The purple dot on the plot marks f_c. Try increasing R and watch it shift left.
1.2: f_c = 1/(2π·R·C). Doubling R halves f_c. Halving C doubles f_c.
1.3: Visit 3 different decades of f_c. Try R = 100 Ω with small C, then large C, then large R.

2.1: You need R·C = 1/(2π·200) ≈ 7.96×10⁻⁴ s. Pick a round C then compute R.
2.3: Or try C = 1 µF and R = 800 Ω. Or C = 10 nF and R = 80 kΩ. All give f_c = 200 Hz.

3.1: Look where the rising curve crosses the horizontal −3 dB line (dashed orange).
3.2: Or find the 'knee' — where the rising sloped part flattens out. That corner is f_c.
3.3: Read the x-axis at that point. It is a log scale: each major tick is a factor of 10.
